tip: 'De aap komt uit de mouw' means the hidden truth or real motive finally comes out: 'nu komt de aap uit de mouw'.
Put 'het' before an infinitive to turn a verb into a noun: 'het opruimen' (the cleaning-up), so 'begonnen met het opruimen' means started the tidying.
'Krijgen te horen' literally means to get to hear, the Dutch way of saying to be told: 'kregen te horen dat' (were told that).
'Hoe de vork in de steel zit' literally means how the fork sits in its handle, and stands for how things really are.
'Slagen in' becomes 'erin slagen', where 'er' points ahead to what you succeed in: 'zij slaagt erin om alles op tijd klaar te krijgen' = she manages to get it done on time.
Separable verbs split around 'te': 'doorwerken' becomes 'door te werken', as in 'zij is te moe om nog langer door te werken'.
The Dutch equivalent of two birds with one stone is two flies in one swat: 'zij vangt twee vliegen in een klap'.
'Om te' plus an infinitive marks purpose, in order to: 'om te studeren' = in order to study.
'Om de hete brij draaien' literally means to circle around the hot porridge, and means to beat around the bush.
'Lekker' isn't only about taste. In 'slaap lekker' it means pleasantly or well, the usual Dutch way to say good night.
'Leuk je te ontmoeten' – 'om' is often omitted in casual speech before 'te' + infinitive.
For sound, 'hard' means loud, not difficult. So 'dat de muziek te hard stond' says that the music was too loud.
Starting with 'nergens' flips subject and verb: it becomes 'vind je', not 'je vindt', keeping the verb in second place.
'Snappen van' wraps around 'er': 'ik snap er niks van' = I understand nothing of it; 'er ... van' points to the topic.
After 'dat', Dutch pushes the verbs to the end: 'dat hij de fout had gemaakt', not 'dat hij had de fout gemaakt'.
'Houden' needs 'van' to mean love: 'dat hij van haar hield' = that he loved her. Without 'van' it means to keep or hold.
'Namens' is formal for 'on behalf of'.
'Zowel ... als' pairs two items, like both ... and: 'zowel de bus als de tram' = both the bus and the tram.
'Prettige' – adjective before a de-word gets -e ending: 'prettige feestdagen'.
'Alles goed met je?' – a casual check-in. The verb 'gaat' is often dropped in informal Dutch.
'Ik ga zo weg' = I'm leaving in a moment: 'zo' is a very casual 'soon'.
'Met zijn mond vol tanden staan' literally means to stand with your mouth full of teeth, and means to be lost for words.
'Gelieve' is extremely formal – mostly used in official and bureaucratic writing.
'Schoonmoeder' = 'schoon' (clean) + 'moeder' (mother) – 'schoon-' means 'in-law' in family terms.
'Gaarne' is extremely formal for 'graag' – mostly in written business Dutch.
'Erop wijzen' is formal; informally you'd say 'even zeggen dat'.
'Met de handen in het haar zitten' literally means to sit with your hands in your hair, and means to be at your wits' end.
'Aangehecht' is formal email language – 'attached herewith'.
The ending '-etje' makes things small; after a short vowel plus 'm' the consonant doubles: 'lam' → 'lammetje'.
'Voorts' is extremely formal for 'verder' or 'ook'.
